steps.user_message: I need advice about my health. I'm 41, with atrial fibrillation managed on levothyroxine 75mcg. My cardiologist is Dr. Lisa Park at Boston Pulmonary; I had a bone density scan last month that was normal. I also have GERD and take metoprolol 25mg. I'm wondering if I should ask about switching to a single-pill combination and whether my recent dizziness could be blood-pressure related. Can you help me prepare questions for my next visit?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with health-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Good — I can help you get ready. Below are suggested questions to bring to your cardiology visit with Dr. Lisa Park, organized by topic, plus short explanations of why each is useful and what you can do beforehand.

Practical prep (bring to the visit)
- A current list of all medications, doses, and when you take them (prescription, OTC, supplements, vitamins).
- Recent home blood pressure readings (ideally morning and evening for a week) and a log of the dizziness episodes (when, what you were doing, how long it lasted, any associated symptoms like palpitations or fainting).
- Last thyroid lab results (TSH/free T4) and your bone density report.

Questions to ask about your medications and a possible single‑pill combination
1. “Would I be a good candidate for a single‑pill combination (SPC) medication for blood pressure — and which combination would you recommend given my atrial fibrillation and current meds?”
   - Why: SPCs can improve adherence but must be compatible with AF and any other indications. There are many SPC types (ACEi/ARB + diuretic or CCB). Beta‑blockers (metoprolol) aren’t always in common SPCs.
2. “Could switching to an SPC affect my AF rate control or symptoms (palpitations, dizziness)?”
   - Why: Some BP meds change heart rate or interact with rate control.
3. “Are there interactions or timing issues between levothyroxine and my GERD medicine (or other medications) that I should change?”
   - Why: Levothyroxine absorption is sensitive to timing and some medications/supplements (PPIs, calcium, iron, antacids). Best practice is usually to take levothyroxine on an empty stomach and separate from those agents.
4. “Is metoprolol 25 mg still the right dose for me? Could it be causing or contributing to my dizziness?”
   - Why: Beta‑blockers can cause low blood pressure or bradycardia that leads to dizziness. Ask about checking pulse/ECG and possibly adjusting dose.
5. “If we consider an SPC, would that replace metoprolol or be added to it?”
   - Why: Clarifies whether the SPC would change your AF management or simply consolidate BP meds.

Questions about the recent dizziness
6. “Could my dizziness be blood‑pressure related (low BP or orthostatic hypotension)? Can we check orthostatic vitals today?”
   - Why: A simple orthostatic check (BP/pulse lying, sitting, standing) can show posture‑related drops.
7. “Should I record my blood pressure and heart rate at home/when dizzy? What targets or thresholds should I report or seek urgent care for?”
   - Why: Gives you measurable values to track and know when to act.
8. “Do you recommend any cardiac monitoring (ECG, 24–48 hour Holter, event monitor, or loop recorder) to evaluate dizziness or intermittent arrhythmia?”
   - Why: Dizziness could relate to intermittent arrhythmias or pauses; ambulatory monitoring can capture that.
9. “Could any of my other conditions (GERD, thyroid dose) or their meds be contributing to dizziness?”
   - Why: Electrolyte shifts, thyroid over‑replacement, or medication interactions can cause symptoms.

Questions about thyroid management and labs
10. “When should my TSH/free T4 be checked next, and could my symptoms be from too much or too little thyroid hormone?”
    - Why: Over‑replacement can cause palpitations/AF symptoms; under‑replacement can cause fatigue. Make sure TSH target is confirmed.
11. “Are there any special instructions for taking levothyroxine with my GERD meds or supplements (calcium/vitamin D)?”
    - Why: Best to separate levothyroxine from calcium/iron by ~4 hours; take levothyroxine 30–60 minutes before breakfast.

Questions about anticoagulation and overall AF care (if not already covered)
12. “Are my stroke‑prevention needs (anticoagulation) up to date for my AF? Is my current regimen still appropriate?”
    - Why: Important part of AF care — you didn’t list an anticoagulant, so confirm whether you’re on one.
13. “Do we need any imaging or testing (echocardiogram, labs) given my AF management and recent symptoms?”
    - Why: Echo or labs (electrolytes, thyroid) may be needed.

Questions about bone health and GERD meds
14. “My bone density was normal last month — any precautions if I need long‑term PPI therapy for GERD?”
    - Why: Long‑term PPI use can affect calcium absorption and bone health; discuss monitoring/supplements.
15. “Should I take calcium or vitamin D supplements? If so, how should I time them with levothyroxine?”
    - Why: Clarify timing to avoid absorption interference.

Logistics and safety
16. “If we change medications (dose or new SPC), how soon should I expect changes in symptoms and how will we monitor for side effects?”
    - Why: Know follow‑up plan and when to call.
17. “What are warning signs that I should seek urgent care or call you (worsening dizziness, fainting, chest pain, sustained palpitations)?”
    - Why: Safety thresholds.

Suggested phrasing you can read at the visit
- “I’ve had several dizzy spells recently. I keep a log of my BP and symptoms — can we check orthostatic vitals and decide whether this is from my meds or needs further monitoring?”
- “I’m taking levothyroxine 75 mcg for thyroid and metoprolol 25 mg — are there any interactions or timing changes I should make because of my GERD medication?”
- “Would a single‑pill combination for my blood pressure be safe and helpful for me? If so, which one and how would it work with my AF medications?”

What you can do before the appointment
- Start a 1–2 week BP log (morning and evening) and note any dizziness episodes with time, position (lying/sitting/standing), and what you’d just eaten or medications taken.
- Note exact names/doses of your GERD medication(s) and any OTC antacids, calcium, or iron supplements.
- Bring lab results (TSH) and bone density report or let the clinic know they’re available.

If you’d like, I can:
- Turn these points into a one‑page printout or an email to Dr. Park’s office.
- Draft wording for a message to ask the clinic to check orthostatic vitals and TSH before the visit.

Which of those would you like me to prepare?
